Abstract classes are meant to be base classes. They cannot be turned into objects

The static keyword means count is shared by all instances. Every time the constructor

question: (Comparison) What is a key difference between an Interface and an Abstract Class in modern Java (post-Java 8)?

options.text: A class can implement multiple Interfaces but can only extend one Abstract Class.

options.label: D

This is the primary architectural difference. Inheritance is limited to one parent (Single
Inheritance), but a class can satisfy multiple "contracts" by implementing many interfaces.

question: (Conceptual) Which of the following best describes Composition over Inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: Using a child class to access parent methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Deleting a class to save memory.

Composition (e.g., a Car class having an Engine object as a field) is often more flexible than
inheritance because it allows you to change behavior at runtime by swapping objects.
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) Why will the following code fail to compile? class Test { int x = 10; static void display() { print(x); } }

options.text: A static method cannot access a non-static (instance) variable.

Static methods exist at the class level. They don't know which specific object's x they should
print, because they can be called even if zero objects of Test have been created.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the purpose of a Constructor?

options.text: To delete an object from memory.

options.label: C
options.text: To make the class run faster.

options.text: To convert a class into an interface.

Constructors are called automatically when new is used. Their job is to set the initial values of
the object's variables.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You are designing a PaymentSystem. You have different types of payments: CreditCard, PayPal, and Crypto. They all must have a process() method. What is the best way to enforce this?

options.label: A
options.text: Copy the process() method into each class.

options.label: B
options.text: Create an interface IPayment with a process() method and make all classes implement it.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a global function that checks the payment type with if-else.

options.label: D
options.text: Make all payment types inherit from CreditCard.

An Interface acts as a contract. It guarantees that any class claiming to be a "Payment" must
have a process() method, allowing you to handle them all uniformly.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) What is Method Overloading?

options.label: A
options.text: Changing the logic of a parent method in a child class.

options.label: B
options.text: Defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters.

options.label: C
options.text: Calling a method too many times in a loop.

explanation:
Overloading allows a class to have, for example, add(int a, int b) and add(double
a, double b). The compiler picks the right one based on the arguments you pass.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the meaning of the final keyword (or sealed in C#) when applied to a **Class**?

options.label: B
options.text: The class cannot be inherited from (it cannot have children).

options.label: C
options.text: All methods in the class are static.

options.label: D
options.text: The class is deleted when the program ends.

Marking a class final prevents other developers from extending it. This is often done for
security or to ensure the class's behavior isn't modified (e.g., the String class in Java is
final).
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) In a User class, the password field is set to private and can only be changed via a setPassword() method that checks for a minimum length. Which OOP principle is being applied?
explanation:
This is "Data Hiding." By making the field private and providing a public method, you control
how the data is accessed and validated, protecting the integrity of the object.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) What will happen if a class does not define a constructor?

options.label: B
options.text: No objects of that class can be created.

options.label: C
options.text: The compiler provides a hidden "Default Constructor" with no parameters.

options.label: D
options.text: The object will have no memory.

explanation:
Most OOP languages provide a default constructor automatically so you can still do new
MyClass(). However, if you define any custom constructor, the default one is removed.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What does the super (or base) keyword do inside a child class constructor?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the child class run faster.

options.label: B
options.text: It calls the constructor of the Parent class.

options.label: D
options.text: It converts the class to an interface.

explanation:
Before a child object is fully created, its parent "part" must be initialized. super() ensures the
parent's constructor runs first.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You have a list of Employee objects. Some are Managers, some are Developers. You want to calculate the total salary by calling emp.getSalary() on every item in the list. This is possible because of:
explanation:
Polymorphism allows you to treat a group of different objects (Managers, Developers) as their
common type (Employee) and call the same method name, while getting the specific behavior
for each.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the difference between Aggregation and Composition?

options.label: C
options.text: In Composition, the child object cannot exist without the parent; in Aggregation, the child can exist independently.

explanation:
Example: A Room is part of a House (Composition - if house is deleted, room is gone). A
Teacher is part of a Department (Aggregation - if department is deleted, teacher still exists).
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) What is a Memory Leak in an OOP language like C++?

options.label: A
options.text: When an object takes too much RAM.

options.label: B
options.text: When an object is created on the heap using 'new' but is never 'deleted', leaving unreachable memory.

options.label: C
options.text: When a variable is used twice.

explanation:
In unmanaged languages, if you lose the pointer to an object on the heap without freeing it,
that memory is "lost" to the system until the program restarts.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is a Virtual Method Table (V-Table) used for?

options.label: A
options.text: To sort objects in a list.

options.label: B
options.text: To support Dynamic Dispatch/Polymorphism by looking up the correct method address at runtime.

options.label: D
options.text: To speed up the compilation process.

explanation:
V-Tables are the internal mechanism that makes polymorphism work. Every object with
overridden methods has a hidden table of pointers to the correct versions of those methods.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) If a class A has a protected member x, who can access it?

options.label: C
options.text: Class A, its subclasses, and classes in the same package.

explanation:
protected is less restrictive than private but more restrictive than public. Its main
purpose is to allow child classes to access parent data.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the Single Responsibility Principle (the S in SOLID)?

options.label: A
options.text: A class should only have one object.

options.label: B
options.text: A class should only have one method.

options.label: C
options.text: A class should have only one reason to change (it should only do one job).

options.label: D
options.text: A class should only be written by one developer.

explanation:
If a class handles both "Database Logic" and "UI Printing," it has two responsibilities.
Changing the UI could accidentally break the Database part. SOLID design says they should
be separate.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You want to prevent a method in a parent class from being overridden by any child class. What keyword should you use?
explanation:
Marking a method final ensures that its implementation is "final" and cannot be changed by
subclasses. (Note: private methods are also effectively final).
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is a Copy Constructor?

options.label: A
options.text: A constructor that copies a class file.

options.label: B
options.text: A constructor that creates a new object as a copy of an existing object.

options.label: C
options.text: A constructor that uses the 'super' keyword.

options.label: D
options.text: A constructor that returns a string.

explanation:
Copy constructors (common in C++) allow you to create Object B using Object A's data,
ensuring a "deep copy" where all values are duplicated.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) In a language like Python, what is the purpose of the self (or this in Java) keyword?

options.label: A
options.text: To refer to the parent class.

options.label: B
options.text: To refer to the current instance of the object.

options.label: D
options.text: To make the code run faster.

explanation:
When a method is called, the computer needs to know which object's data to use. this or
self acts as a pointer to the specific object that called the method.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In the standard memory layout of a C/C++ program, which segment grows downward (towards lower addresses) during function calls?
explanation:
In most architectures, the Stack grows downward from high memory addresses, while the
Heap grows upward from low addresses. This "growing towards each other" design
maximizes the use of available space.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A Java application is running, and the RAM usage is steadily increasing. Suddenly, the usage drops by 500MB without any user action. What most likely occurred?

options.label: B
options.text: A Memory Leak was fixed automatically.

options.label: C
options.text: The Garbage Collector (GC) triggered a "Major Collection" cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: The program moved variables from the Heap to the Stack.

explanation:
Garbage Collection is non-deterministic; it runs when the JVM decides memory is low. A
sudden drop in RAM usage indicates that the GC has successfully reclaimed memory from
unreachable objects.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing / C++) What is the danger in the following code snippet? int* ptr = new int(10); ptr = new int(20);
explanation:
The first line allocates memory for an integer (10) on the heap. The second line makes ptr
point to a new integer (20). The memory for "10" is still allocated, but we no longer have a
pointer to it, so it can never be deleted. This is a memory leak.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the primary functional difference between malloc() in C and new in C++?

options.label: B
options.text: new allocates memory AND calls the object's constructor; malloc() only allocates raw bytes.

options.label: C
options.text: malloc() handles objects; new handles primitives.

explanation:
new is an operator that is "object-aware." It calculates the size needed and automatically
initializes the object. malloc() is a function that returns a void* and knows nothing about
the data type being stored.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) Which Garbage Collection algorithm works by keeping a count of how many pointers refer to an object, and deleting the object when the count reaches zero?
explanation:
Reference Counting is simple but has a major flaw: it cannot handle "Circular References"
(where Object A points to B, and B points to A, keeping both counts at 1 even if the rest of the
program has forgotten them).
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) What typically causes a Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV)?

options.label: B
options.text: A logical error in a math formula.

options.label: C
options.text: Attempting to access a memory address that the program does not have permission to access (e.g., dereferencing a NULL pointer).

explanation:
The OS protects memory. If your program tries to read or write to an address that hasn't been
assigned to it (like address 0x0), the OS kills the process with a Segmentation Fault to
prevent system corruption.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In modern Garbage Collectors, what is the "Generational Hypothesis"?

options.label: A
options.text: Older objects are more likely to be deleted.

options.label: B
options.text: Most objects "die young" (become unreachable quickly after creation).

options.label: C
options.text: Memory should be divided by the generation of the CPU.

options.label: D
options.text: Objects created by loops are permanent.

explanation:
Observation shows that most objects are temporary (local variables, temporary strings). GCs
use this by dividing the heap into "Young" and "Old" generations, scanning the "Young" area
much more frequently to improve performance.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A C++ developer uses std::unique_ptr instead of raw pointers. This is an application of which memory management philosophy?
explanation:
Smart pointers like unique_ptr use RAII. When the smart pointer object goes out of scope
(e.g., a function ends), its destructor is called, which automatically deletes the heap memory it
was managing.
subject: Programming

question: (Calculation) If a 32-bit system has a maximum of 4GB of addressable memory, how many bits are used for each memory address?
explanation:
2^32 equals approximately 4.29 billion. Therefore, a 32-bit address can uniquely identify 4.29
billion individual bytes (4GB). This is why 32-bit operating systems cannot use more than 4GB
of RAM.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is Memory Fragmentation?

options.label: B
options.text: When the CPU cache is full.

options.label: C
options.text: When free memory is broken into small, non-contiguous blocks, making it impossible to allocate a large continuous object even if total free space is sufficient.

options.label: D
options.text: When the Stack and Heap collide.

explanation:
Fragmentation occurs over time as objects of different sizes are allocated and deleted.
"Compaction" is the process where a Garbage Collector moves objects around to group free
space back into one large block.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In the Java/C# exception hierarchy, which type of exception usually represents a programmer's logic error and does not need to be explicitly declared in the method signature?
explanation:
Unchecked exceptions (like NullPointerException or ArithmeticException) are
typically the result of bad logic. Since they can happen anywhere, the language doesn't force
you to declare them, unlike Checked exceptions (I/O, SQL).
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) What is the output of the following pseudocode? function check(): try: print("A") return 1 catch: print("B") finally: print("C")
explanation:
The finally block is guaranteed to run. Even if the try block encounters a return, the
execution "pauses," runs the finally code, and then completes the return.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer writes a catch (Exception e) { } block with no code inside. Why is this considered "Dangerous" in professional software development?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the program run slower.

options.label: B
options.text: It "swallows" the exception, hiding the fact that an error occurred and making debugging impossible.

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents the finally block from running.

explanation:
Ignoring an exception means the program may continue in an unstable or corrupted state
without any log or error message to help the developer find the root cause.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the primary difference between throw and throws?

options.label: B
options.text: throw is used to actually trigger an exception; throws is used in the method header to declare potential exceptions.

options.label: C
options.text: throws is for errors; throw is for exceptions.

options.label: D
options.text: throw is used in Python; throws is used in Java.

explanation:
throw new Exception() is an action. void myMethod() throws IOException is a
declaration (a warning to the caller).
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) Look at this C++ catch sequence. Why is it problematic? try { ... } catch (std::exception& e) { ... } catch (std::runtime_error& e) { ... }

options.label: A
options.text: You cannot have two catch blocks.

options.label: B
options.text: The second block is unreachable because runtime_error is a child of exception.

options.label: D
options.text: It will cause a compiler crash.

explanation:
Exceptions must be caught from "Most Specific" to "Most General." Since runtime_error is
a type of exception, the first block will catch everything, leaving the second block useless.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What happens if an exception is thrown inside a function, but there is no try-catch block to handle it in that function?

options.label: B
options.text: The exception "bubbles up" (propagates) to the calling function in the stack.

explanation:
This is "Exception Propagation." The runtime searches down the call stack for a handler. If it
reaches the main() method and still finds no handler, only then does the program terminate.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You are writing a banking app. A user tries to withdraw $100 but only has $50. Which is the most appropriate way to handle this?

options.label: D
options.text: Use a while loop to wait for more money.

explanation:
Custom exceptions make code more readable and allow the calling logic to specifically handle
"Business Rule" violations differently than "Technical Errors."
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) Trace the result of this Java-style math logic: try: int x = 10 / 0 catch (ArithmeticException e): x = 0 print(x)

In many languages (like Java/C#), variables declared inside a try block are local to that
block. x cannot be accessed in the catch block or the print statement unless it was
declared before the try block.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) Which of the following is true regarding Errors (like java.lang.Error)?

options.label: A
options.text: They should be caught using a try-catch block.

options.label: B
options.text: They are the same as Runtime Exceptions.

options.label: C
options.text: They represent serious problems that an application should usually not try to catch.

options.label: D
options.text: They are caused by user input.

Errors (like VirtualMachineError) indicate that the environment is broken. Trying to
"catch" and continue from these is usually futile and dangerous.

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer needs to ensure a Database connection is closed even if an SQL error occurs. Which block is dedicated to this "cleanup" logic?

The finally block is the "Cleanup" zone. Whether the operation succeeded or failed, you
must release external resources like DB connections, File handles, or Network sockets.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) Why is it generally considered bad practice to use Exceptions for standard "Control Flow" (e.g., using an exception to break out of a loop)?

options.label: B
options.text: Generating an exception is computationally expensive because it requires capturing the entire stack trace.

options.label: C
options.text: Exceptions only work for mathematical errors.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the code run too fast for the user.

explanation:
Exceptions are for "Exceptional" (unusual) cases. Creating an exception object involves
"Stack Walking" to fill the stack trace, which is a very heavy CPU operation. Standard logic
should use if-else or break.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) In a language like Python, what is the equivalent of the catch block?
explanation:
Python uses try...except...finally. Ruby uses begin...rescue...ensure.
Though keywords vary, the logic remains identical across OOP languages.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You are using a try-with-resources block (Java) to read a file. When does the file.close() method get called?

options.label: B
options.text: Only if the file is read successfully.

options.label: C
options.text: Automatically at the end of the block, regardless of success or failure.

options.label: D
options.text: Never; you must call it manually.

try-with-resources is "Syntactic Sugar" that ensures any object implementing
AutoCloseable is closed automatically, preventing resource leaks.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is a "Nested" try-catch block?

options.label: B
options.text: A try-catch block placed inside another try or catch block.

options.label: C
options.text: A try-catch block that handles two different types of exceptions.

options.label: D
options.text: A try-catch block written in a child class.

explanation:
Nesting is used when a recovery step (inside a catch block) might itself cause an error (e.g.,
trying to log an error to a database, but the database is also down).
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) A program crashes with a "Stack Overflow Error." This is most likely caused by:

options.label: B
options.text: Trying to access index 10 of a size-5 array.

options.label: C
options.text: A recursive function that never hits its base case.

options.label: D
options.text: Creating an object that is too large for the Heap.

explanation:
Every function call takes up space on the Stack. Infinite recursion fills this space until the
system throws a StackOverflowError.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the primary purpose of a Namespace in languages like C++, C#, or PHP?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the code run faster.

options.label: B
options.text: To prevent naming conflicts by grouping related identifiers under a unique name.

options.label: D
options.text: To manage the hardware's memory allocation.

explanation:
Namespaces allow you to have a Database.Connect() and a Network.Connect() in
the same project. Without namespaces, the compiler wouldn't know which Connect()
function you are referring to.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is a major disadvantage of using a Static Library compared to a Dynamic Library?

options.label: B
options.text: It requires a separate file to be present during execution.

options.label: C
options.text: It increases the size of the executable file and requires a full re-compile to update the library code.

Because static libraries are physically "baked into" your .exe, any update to the library
means you must rebuild your entire app. Dynamic libraries (DLLs) can be updated
independently without touching the main executable.

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer is using npm for a JavaScript project and pip for a Python project. These tools are best classified as:
explanation:
Package managers automate the process of installing, upgrading, configuring, and removing
software libraries (dependencies) that your project needs to function.

explanation:
When you use a Library, you call its functions. When you use a Framework, you plug your
code into its "slots," and the framework decides when to call your code. This reversal of the
calling flow is called IoC.
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) You are trying to compile a project, but the compiler says "Module not found" or "Include file missing," even though the code is perfect. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: A syntax error in the main function.

options.label: B
options.text: A logical error in a loop.

options.label: C
options.text: The "Library Path" or "Search Path" is not correctly configured in the build settings.

options.label: D
options.text: The computer has run out of RAM.

Compilers don't search the whole computer for files. You must explicitly tell the compiler which
folders contain the external modules or header files your code depends on.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) Look at this Java import: import java.util.*;. What does the * signify?

options.label: A
options.text: Import only the classes that contain math.

options.label: B
options.text: Import every class in the entire Java language.

options.label: C
options.text: Import all public classes within the java.util package.

The wildcard * tells the compiler to make every class in that specific package available for use
in the current file.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is a Circular Dependency?

options.label: B
options.text: When two or more modules depend on each other directly or indirectly, creating a cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: When an object inherits from its own child.

Circular dependencies make systems "brittle." If Module A needs B to compile, but B needs A
to compile, the compiler cannot decide which one to build first, leading to a "chicken and egg"
problem.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) In C/C++, what is the role of a Header File (.h) compared to a Source File (.cpp)?

options.text: Header files contain the actual logic; Source files contain only comments.

options.text: Header files contain declarations (signatures); Source files contain definitions (implementations).

options.text: Header files are only for global variables.

options.label: D
options.text: Source files are used at runtime; Header files are for compilation.

Header files act as the "Public Interface." They tell other modules "These functions exist,"
while the source files contain the secret "How it works" code.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You want to share your code so that other developers can use it, but you don't want them to see your actual source code. How should you distribute your logic?

options.label: B
options.text: As a pre-compiled Library (e.g., .jar, .dll, or .a file).

options.label: C
options.text: As a screenshots of your IDE.

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot share code without sharing the source.

Libraries allow you to distribute code in its compiled (binary) form. Other developers can link
their programs against your library and use your functions without ever seeing your original
logic.

question: (Conceptual) Which of the following is an example of Semantic Versioning (SemVer)?

SemVer is the industry standard for libraries. Major (breaking changes), Minor (new features,
no breaks), and Patch (bug fixes). This allows developers to safely automate updates.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the primary advantage of using Generics over using the Object class to store items in a collection?

options.text: It makes the collection take up less RAM.

options.label: B
options.text: It provides compile-time type safety, eliminating the need for manual type casting and preventing runtime ClassCastExceptions.

options.text: It allows the collection to store both primitives and objects simultaneously.

(using Object), you could accidentally put an Integer in, and the program would crash only
when you try to read it later.

"Integer" part; the compiler just inserts hidden casts everywhere you access the list.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You are using a modern Web Framework that automatically creates a database table based on your class name and variable names. Which advanced concept is the framework using to "read" your code?

Reflection allows a framework (like Spring, Hibernate, or Entity Framework) to "look" at your
class at runtime, see that you named a variable userName, and then generate the SQL
CREATE TABLE command automatically.

1. filter(x > 2) keeps only [3, 4].

question: (Conceptual) What is a Closure in programming?

options.label: A
options.text: A function that closes a file handle automatically.

options.label: B
options.text: A function (usually a lambda) that carries with it the environment (variables) of the scope in which it was created.

options.label: C
options.text: The final line of a program.

options.label: D

lambda can still access those variables because it has "captured" them.

question: (Debugging) Why is Reflection often discouraged in performance-critical sections of an application (like the inner loop of a game engine)?

options.label: B
options.text: It involves significant CPU overhead due to metadata lookups and dynamic type checking that cannot be optimized by the compiler.

explanation:
Standard method calls are mapped to direct memory addresses during compilation. Reflection
requires the CPU to search through string tables of method names at runtime, which is much
slower.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the difference between C++ Templates and Java Generics?

options.label: A
options.text: C++ Templates generate a new copy of the code for every type used (Monomorphization); Java uses a single copy of code and erases types.

options.label: C
options.text: C++ Templates only work with integers.

explanation:
C++ creates a vector_int and a vector_double internally. This makes the binary larger
but very fast. Java uses one List and treats everything as Object, which is slower but
keeps the file size smaller.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer adds @Deprecated to a method in Java or [Obsolete] in C#. What is the purpose of this metadata?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the method run faster.

options.label: B
options.text: To warn other developers that the method is outdated and should no longer be used.

options.label: C
options.text: To hide the method from the public API.

options.label: D
options.text: To automatically delete the method during the next build.

explanation:
These are Annotations/Attributes. They don't change the logic, but they provide info to the
compiler to generate warnings and to IDEs to cross out the method name for the user.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) Look at this C++ Template snippet: template <typename T> T add(T a, T b) { return a + b; } print(add(5, 10)); print(add(2.5, 1.5)); What is the output?
explanation:
The template generates an int version for the first call (15) and a double version for the
second call (4.0). Templates provide powerful type-specific logic.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In functional programming, what does the Reduce (or Fold) operation do?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes elements from a list.

options.label: B
options.text: It combines all elements of a collection into a single value (e.g., calculating a sum) using a specific accumulator function.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the code file smaller.

options.label: D
options.text: It converts a list into a set.

explanation:
Reduce takes a list [1, 2, 3] and a function (a, b) -> a + b and returns 6. It
"reduces" the collection to a single result.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You want to write a function that can accept any List, but you want to ensure the items in the list are at least a type of Animal (e.g., Dog or Cat). Which concept should you use?

options.label: B
options.text: Bounded Wildcards / Generic Constraints (e.g., <T extends Animal>)

explanation:
Bounded generics (Constraints) allow you to restrict the types that can be used with a generic
class, ensuring that they share a specific parent or interface.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is Introspection in the context of advanced programming?

options.label: A
options.text: When a developer reviews their own code.

options.label: B
options.text: The specific part of Reflection that allows a program to examine its own properties (like checking if a class has a certain method).

options.label: C
options.text: When a program predicts its own crash.

options.label: D
options.text: A tool for measuring CPU temperature.

explanation:
Introspection is the "read-only" part of Reflection. It's used to discover the capabilities of an
object at runtime without changing them.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) Trace the value of result: def multiplier(factor): return lambda x : x * factor triple = multiplier(3) result = triple(10)
explanation:
multiplier(3) returns a closure where factor is 3. When triple(10) is called, it
executes 10 * 3, resulting in 30.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the main purpose of Fluent Interfaces (Method Chaining), often seen in advanced libraries?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the code run faster.

options.label: B
options.text: To improve code readability by allowing multiple method calls to be linked in a single "sentence-like" instruction.

options.label: D
options.text: To use only one variable for the whole program.

explanation:
Method chaining (e.g., object.setName("A").setAge(20).save();) creates a "Fluent
API" that is very popular in modern Java and JavaScript libraries for configuration.
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) Why might a Closure cause a memory leak in a language with Garbage Collection?

options.label: B
options.text: A long-lived closure might hold a reference to a large object from its outer scope, preventing that object from being garbage collected.

options.label: C
options.text: Closures use the hard drive instead of RAM.

options.label: D
options.text: Closures are only stored in the CPU cache.

explanation:
Because a closure "captures" variables, those variables stay alive as long as the closure
exists. If you store a small lambda in a global list but it captures a 1GB object, that 1GB stays
in RAM forever.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) Which of the following best describes the difference between a Process and a Thread?

options.label: A
options.text: Processes share the same memory; threads do not.

options.label: B
options.text: Threads of the same process share the Heap memory but have individual Stacks; Processes have isolated memory.

options.label: C
options.text: Threads are managed by the hardware; processes are managed by the programmer.

options.label: D
options.text: A process can only have one thread.

explanation:
Threads are "lightweight processes." Because they share the same heap, they can
communicate very quickly, but they risk corrupting shared data. Processes are isolated by the
OS for security and stability.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) Two threads both execute count = count + 1 at the exact same time. The initial value is 0. After both finish, the value is 1 instead of 2. This is a classic example of:
explanation:
Both threads read 0, incremented it to 1, and wrote it back. Because the operation was not
Atomic or Synchronized, one increment was lost.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing / Logic) Trace the result of using a Mutex (Lock) in this pseudocode: Thread A: Lock(m); x = x + 1; Unlock(m); Thread B: Lock(m); x = x + 1; Unlock(m); If x starts at 0, what is the guaranteed result?
explanation:
The Mutex ensures that only one thread can be in the "Critical Section" (x = x + 1) at a time. If
Thread A has the lock, Thread B must wait until A unlocks it. This guarantees a correct sum of
2.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What are the four necessary conditions for a Deadlock to occur (Coffman conditions)?

options.label: C
options.text: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.

explanation:
If you break any one of these four conditions (e.g., by allowing resources to be taken away/
preempted), a Deadlock becomes mathematically impossible.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the difference between a Mutex and a Semaphore?

options.label: A
options.text: Mutex is for integers; Semaphore is for strings.

options.label: B
options.text: A Mutex is a binary lock (only 1 thread); a Semaphore is a counter that can allow a specific number (N) of threads to access a resource.

options.label: C
options.text: Semaphores are only used in Python.

explanation:
Think of a Mutex as a bathroom key (1 person). Think of a Semaphore as a restaurant with 10
tables (10 people can enter; the 11th must wait).
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) An application is designed to use 100 threads on a 4-core CPU. The developer notices the app is actually slower than the single-threaded version. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: B
options.text: High Context Switching overhead and Thread Contention.

options.label: D
options.text: Threads do not work on 4-core CPUs.

explanation:
The CPU has to constantly save and load the state of 100 threads. If the tasks are very short,
the "management time" (Context Switching) exceeds the "work time," leading to poor
performance.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What does it mean for a function or class to be "Thread-Safe"?

options.label: A
options.text: It runs only on one thread.

options.label: B
options.text: It functions correctly during simultaneous execution by multiple threads without data corruption.

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot be deleted by the OS.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses the safe keyword in C++.

explanation:
Thread-safety is achieved through synchronization (locks), using immutable data, or using
"Atomic" variables that handle concurrency at the hardware level.
subject: Programming

question: (Code-Tracing) In Java/C#, what is the effect of calling thread.join()?

options.label: B
options.text: It makes two threads run in parallel.

options.label: C
options.text: The calling thread pauses execution until the thread being "joined" has finished its work.

options.label: D
options.text: It merges two threads into one.

explanation:
Join is used for synchronization. If the Main thread calls Worker.join(), the Main thread
will wait at that line until the Worker thread terminates.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is Amdahl's Law used to predict?

options.label: A
options.text: The amount of RAM needed for a thread.

options.label: B
options.text: The theoretical maximum speedup of a program when using multiple processors, limited by the portion of the program that is strictly sequential.

explanation:
If 50% of your code must run in a specific order (sequential), then even with an infinite number
of processors, you can never speed up the program by more than 2x.
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) You have two threads that are constantly changing their state in response to each other, but neither is making any progress toward finishing. This is called:
explanation:
In a Livelock, threads are not "blocked" (waiting), but they are stuck in a loop of reacting to
each other (like two people in a hallway trying to step out of each other's way but moving in
the same direction repeatedly).
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In the "Red-Green-Refactor" cycle of Test-Driven Development (TDD), what does the "Red" stage represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The program has a syntax error.

options.label: C
options.text: Writing a test for a new feature that fails because the feature hasn't been implemented yet.

explanation:
In TDD, you write the test first. Since the functionality doesn't exist yet, the test must fail
(Red). This ensures the test is actually checking the right thing once the code is written.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer makes a small change to the "Login" logic. Suddenly, the "Checkout" page stops working. Which type of testing would have caught this?
explanation:
Regression testing involves running all existing test cases after a change to ensure that new
code hasn't "regressed" or broken old, working functionality.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the primary difference between a Breakpoint and a Watchpoint during debugging?

options.label: A
options.text: Breakpoints are for Java; Watchpoints are for C++.

options.label: B
options.text: A Breakpoint pauses execution at a specific line of code; a Watchpoint pauses execution when a specific variable's value changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Watchpoints make the code run faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Breakpoints are only used for syntax errors.

explanation:
Use a Breakpoint when you know where the error is. Use a Watchpoint when you know which
variable is being corrupted but don't know which line of code is changing it.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In software testing, what is Boundary Value Analysis?

options.label: A
options.text: Testing the program on different operating systems.

options.label: B
options.text: Testing the speed of the database.

options.label: C
options.text: Testing inputs at the extreme ends of their allowable range (e.g., testing 0, 1, 99, and 100 for a range of 1-100).

explanation:
Most logical errors (like off-by-one errors) happen at the boundaries of ranges. Testing the
minimum, maximum, and values just outside them is a highly effective testing strategy.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You are optimizing a function that calculates prime numbers. You decide to store previously calculated results in a Hash Map to avoid recalculating them. This optimization is known as:
explanation:
Memoization is a specific form of caching used in dynamic programming. It trades memory
(Space) for speed (Time) by storing the results of expensive function calls.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What does Cyclomatic Complexity measure in a piece of code?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of lines of code.

options.label: B
options.text: The memory usage of the function.

options.label: C
options.text: The number of independent logical paths through the code (IFs, Loops, Cases).

options.label: D
options.text: How many developers worked on the file.

explanation:
Higher cyclomatic complexity means the code has many branches and is harder to test and
maintain. A complexity score of over 10 is usually considered a "Code Smell."
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) What is a "Heisenbug"?

options.label: A
options.text: A bug that only happens in Python.

options.label: B
options.text: A bug that seems to disappear or change its behavior when you attempt to study or debug it.

options.label: C
options.text: A bug caused by a hardware failure.

options.label: D
options.text: A bug that is found by an end-user.

explanation:
These often occur in multi-threaded code or timing-sensitive logic. The act of adding a print
statement or using a debugger changes the timing of the system, making the bug vanish.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) An application works perfectly for 1 user, but the response time becomes 30 seconds when 1,000 users log in. Which tool should the developer use to find the cause?
explanation:
A Profiler tracks execution time and memory usage per function. It would reveal which specific
part of the code (e.g., a slow DB query) is causing the bottleneck under high load.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the purpose of an Assertion (e.g., assert x > 0) in programming?

options.label: A
options.text: To print data to the user.

options.label: B
options.text: To state a condition that must be true at a specific point in the code; if false, the program terminates immediately to signal a bug.

explanation:
Assertions are "Internal checks" for developers. They are used to catch "impossible" states
during development. They are often disabled in the final production release.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the difference between Alpha Testing and Beta Testing?

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha is done by internal employees; Beta is done by a group of real external users.

options.label: B
options.text: Alpha is for mobile; Beta is for web.

options.label: C
options.text: Beta testing is done before Alpha testing.

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha testing checks for security; Beta checks for speed.

explanation:
Alpha testing is the final internal check. Beta testing is a "Field Test" where the software is
released to a limited audience of real users to find bugs in real-world environments.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) Which optimization technique involves replacing a function call with the actual body of the function during compilation?
explanation:
Inlining eliminates the overhead of jumping to a new memory address and setting up a stack
frame. It is great for tiny, frequently called functions but increases binary size.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A developer uses a "Mock Object" during a Unit Test. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the test run on a different server.

options.label: B
options.text: To simulate a complex dependency (like a Database or API) so the unit can be tested in isolation.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the real object is too small.

explanation:
Unit tests should be independent. If you want to test "calculateTotal()", you shouldn't need a
real database. You use a "Mock" that just returns a fixed number when asked for a price.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is Fuzz Testing (Fuzzing)?

options.label: A
options.text: Testing the program with very simple inputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Providing massive amounts of random, invalid, or unexpected data to a program to find security vulnerabilities or crashes.

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring the sound the CPU makes.

explanation:
Fuzzing is an automated technique used to find buffer overflows and logic gaps by
bombarding an input field with millions of "garbage" combinations.
subject: Programming

question: (Debugging) You see a "Core Dump" file after a C++ program crashes. What does this file contain?

options.label: A
options.text: A copy of the source code.

options.label: B
options.text: A snapshot of the program's memory (RAM) at the exact moment it crashed.

options.label: C
options.text: A list of all user passwords.

options.label: D
options.text: The instructions to restart the computer.

explanation:
A Core Dump allows a developer to "post-mortem" debug. You can load the file into a
debugger to see exactly what the values of all variables were when the crash happened.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) A linter flags a "Dead Code" warning. What does this mean?

options.label: B
options.text: The code is written in an old language.

options.label: C
options.text: The code can never be reached or executed during the program's run (e.g., code after a return).

explanation:
Dead code (unreachable code) litters the codebase, increases file size, and confuses other
developers. It should be removed.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In Git, what is the state of a newly created file that has not yet been added to the staging area?
explanation:
A new file is "Untracked" by Git until you run git add. Once added, it becomes "Staged."
After git commit, it is stored in the local repository.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) Two developers edit the exact same line of the same file and try to merge their changes. Git stops the process and asks for help. This situation is called a:
explanation:
Git is smart, but it cannot decide which version of a specific line is "correct." A human must
manually resolve the conflict by picking the right code and committing the result.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is the primary goal of Continuous Integration (CI)?

options.label: A
options.text: To deploy code to the user as fast as possible.

options.label: B
options.text: To detect bugs early by automatically building and testing the code every time a developer commits a change.

options.label: C
options.text: To prevent developers from working on the same file.

options.label: D
options.text: To encrypt the source code repository.

explanation:
CI ensures that the "Main" branch is always healthy. If a developer pushes code that breaks a
test, the CI server flags it immediately before the bug can reach production.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) In a Scrum team, the developers meet for 15 minutes every morning to discuss: 1) What they did yesterday, 2) What they will do today, and 3) Any blockers. This is called:
explanation:
The Daily Standup is a "sync" meeting designed to keep the team aligned and identify
obstacles quickly.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is a major advantage of Distributed Version Control (like Git) over Centralized Version Control (like SVN)?

options.label: B
options.text: Developers can work, commit, and view history offline because they have a full copy of the repository on their own machine.

options.label: C
options.text: It is only compatible with Linux.

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents merge conflicts from happening.

explanation:
In a distributed system, you don't need a constant internet connection to the server to check
the history or save your progress. You only need the server when you want to push or pull.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What is a "Pull Request" (or Merge Request)?

options.label: A
options.text: A request for a salary increase.

options.label: B
options.text: A command to download code from a server.

options.label: C
options.text: A formal request to merge changes from one branch into another, usually involving a code review process.

options.label: D
options.text: A request to restart the server.

explanation:
Pull Requests are the heart of professional collaboration. They allow other team members to
review your code, suggest changes, and ensure quality before the code is officially merged.
subject: Programming

question: (Scenario-Based) You accidentally committed a sensitive API key to a public GitHub repository. What is the safest way to fix this?

options.label: A
options.text: Delete the file and commit again.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the file and commit again.

options.label: C
options.text: Invalidate/Rotate the API key immediately and then use a tool to scrub the history of the repository.

explanation:
Simply deleting the key in a new commit is not enough because the key remains visible in the
previous commits in the history. You must rotate the key (make it useless) and then clean the
history.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) In software maintenance, what is **"Perfective Maintenance"**?

options.label: A
options.text: Fixing a crash reported by a user.

options.label: B
options.text: Improving the performance or maintainability of the software without changing its functionality (e.g., refactoring).

options.label: C
options.text: Updating the software to work on a new OS.

options.label: D
options.text: Adding a new feature requested by a client.

explanation:
Perfective maintenance is about making the software "better" internally—optimizing speed,
cleaning code, or improving the UI—to provide a better experience.
subject: Programming

question: (Comparison) What is the difference between Git Revert and Git Reset --hard?

options.label: B
options.text: Revert creates a new "undo" commit; Reset deletes commits and changes the actual history.

options.label: C
options.text: Reset is safer for shared branches.

options.label: D
options.text: Revert is only for single files.

explanation:
Revert is the "Professional" way to undo. It keeps the history intact. Reset is the
"Destructive" way; if you reset a branch that others have already downloaded, you will break
their local versions.
subject: Programming

question: (Conceptual) What does the term "Definition of Done" (DoD) mean in professional software development?

options.label: A
options.text: The developer finished typing the code.

options.label: B
options.text: The code was pushed to GitHub.

options.label: C
options.text: A checklist of requirements (e.g., code reviewed, tests passed, documented) that must be met before a task is considered finished.

options.label: D
options.text: The project is sold to a customer.

explanation:
DoD prevents "it works on my machine" syndrome. It ensures that quality standards are met
for every single feature before it is officially called "done."
subject: Programming
